desc:
A country has n cities numbered 0 to n - 1 and two-way roads roads[i] = [a, b, len]: driving along the road uses exactly len units of fuel. Fuel is sold in every city v at prices[v] per unit, and you may buy any whole number of units there as long as the tank (capacity cap units) does not overflow. You may pass through a city without buying anything, and you may visit a city more than once.

You start in city 0 with an empty tank and want to reach city n - 1. Return the minimum total amount of money you must spend on fuel, or -1 if the trip is impossible. If n == 1 the answer is 0. Fuel left in the tank at the end is wasted.

n = 4, cap = 4, prices = [3, 1, 2, 9]
roads = [[0,1,2], [1,2,3], [2,3,1], [0,3,6]]
buy 2 units in city 0 (cost 6), drive to city 1; buy 4 units there (cost 4),
drive to city 2 (3 units); buy nothing more: 1 unit is left, drive to city 3
-> 10
hints: Knowing only the current city is not enough: the best decision depends on how much fuel you have. What should a 'state' contain?
Use states (city, fuel) with 0 ≤ fuel ≤ cap. There are at most 100 x 101 of them, and moving between them has a cost: buying one unit of fuel costs prices[city], driving costs nothing in money.

Run Dijkstra over these states. From (v, f) you can go to (v, f + 1) for prices[v] (if f < cap), or along each road (v, u, len) with f ≥ len to (u, f - len) for free. The answer is the cheapest popped state with city n - 1.
editorial: Add the fuel level to the vertex: the state graph has up to n * (cap + 1) = 10,100 vertices. Edges are of two kinds: 'buy one unit' from (v, f) to (v, f + 1) with weight prices[v], and 'drive' from (v, f) to (u, f - len) with weight 0 when enough fuel is available. All weights are non-negative, so Dijkstra gives the minimum money spent.

Buying one unit at a time loses no generality: any purchase of k units is k consecutive single-unit purchases, and the tank bound is checked at every step. Since you never gain by carrying leftover fuel except to use it later, Dijkstra will naturally prefer to fill up cheaply in cheap cities and just enough in expensive ones.

The first time a state (n - 1, f) is popped, its cost is the answer (any fuel level is fine at the end). If the heap empties first, there is no way to arrive, for example because some required road is longer than cap. Time O(n * cap * (deg + 1) * log), which is about 105 heap operations here.
